metadata.title: Rep. Ilhan Omar’s lawyers say authorities ignored judge’s restrictions on home search

sources.news_title: US Rep. Ilhan Omar challenges legality of FBI home search: WSJ
sources.text:
Berk Kutay Gokmen
17 October 2026•Update: 17 October 2026
The defense of US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar have challenged the legality of a search of her Washington home, demanding that federal prosecutors immediately return all seized property and provide recordings made during the operation, The Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday.
In a letter sent late Friday, the Minnesota Democrat’s legal team argued that the search, conducted by Homeland Security Investigations agents early Monday under a federal judge-approved warrant, was “neither justified nor lawful.”
According to the Journal, the investigation focuses partly on how Omar, 44, obtained US citizenship after arriving from Somalia decades ago.
“There is no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status,” the letter said.
Her lawyers alleged that agents failed to follow the judge’s instructions, including a requirement to notify the US House general counsel before executing the warrant. They also said Omar and her attorneys were not given a copy of the warrant beforehand, as ordered by the judge.
The letter claimed agents prevented Omar from contacting her lawyers for more than an hour after the search began.
A Justice Department spokeswoman rejected the allegations, describing the letter as “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies. Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do.”
Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for Washington, defended the operation earlier this week, saying it had been approved by a federal judge mindful of constitutional protections.
“That judge would not have signed that warrant unless there was probable cause,” Pirro said on Fox News.
Omar’s lawyers also accused prosecutors of abusing the grand jury process through subpoenas issued in Washington and Minnesota.
“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the president’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers,” the letter said.
The search came three weeks before November’s midterm elections, in which Omar is seeking a fifth term.
The letter also accused the Justice Department of violating its longstanding practice of avoiding public investigative actions involving political candidates within 60 days of an election, a measure intended to prevent the appearance of partisan interference. Department officials have denied violating any policy.
“This search—which arose from a years-old, tired conspiracy theory concerning conduct stretching back decades—violated longstanding Justice Department policy concerning interference in elections,” the letter said.
Omar has long been targeted by President Donald Trump and conservatives, as well as GOP-led congressional investigations.

sources.news_title: Attorneys for Rep. Ilhan Omar accuse DOJ of violating judge's orders to follow protocols to protect her rights as member of Congress
sources.text:
Attorneys for Rep. Ilhan Omar accuse DOJ of violating judge's orders to follow protocols to protect her rights as member of Congress
Attorneys for Representative Ilhan Omar have accused the Justice Department of violating a magistrate judge's order by failing to follow certain protocols designed to safeguard her constitutional interests as a member of Congress during the search of her home in Washington, D.C.
In the Oct. 16 letter, Omar's attorneys Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz asked the government to immediately return the congresswoman's property, and they also demanded all video and audio recordings of the search be preserved.
"This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the President's chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar's constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers," they wrote in the letter, which was reviewed by CBS News.
In a statement, a Justice Department spokesperson disputed the claims in the letter, saying it was "riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies."
"Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do," the spokesperson said. "Leaking a letter to the press right after sending it is not good faith. It is a publicity play."
Agents from the Homeland Security Investigations executed a search warrant at Omar's home on Monday, as part of a sprawling criminal investigation into her family's history for evidence of possible fraud and false statements in their immigration paperwork.
Her personal cellphone was among the materials seized in the search, CBS News previously reported, and grand jury subpoenas were also issued just days before the search to some of Omar's family members.
The search warrant was first presented to a magistrate judge in U.S. District Court about a week before it was executed.
Prosecutors and the judge engaged in a lengthy back-and-forth, after the judge raised concerns that the search warrant failed to incorporate any protocols to protect Omar's legislative privileges under the Constitution's speech and debate clause, CBS News previously reported.
Those protections stem from the 2007 United States v. Rayburn House Office Building D.C. Circuit Court case, which held that in a criminal investigation of a sitting member of Congress, the executive branch can't review information that is seized in a search without allowing that member to first screen it for legislative privilege.
Initially, prosecutors tried to argue the case shouldn't apply because the search was being carried out at Omar's home, and not at her congressional office, CBS News previously reported.
In the letter to the Justice Department, Omar's lawyers alleged several key requirements imposed by the judge had been violated.
HSI agents, for example, were supposed to notify both Omar and the House of Representatives Office of General Counsel of the execution of the search warrant — a step Omar's lawyers say never took place.
Agents also allegedly prevented her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour after the search started, the letter alleges, even though she and her counsel were supposed to be presented with a copy of the search warrant at the outset.
The timing of the search warrant and issuance of grand jury subpoenas in the case have raised eyebrows among many veteran former prosecutors.
Such overt investigative steps involving a sitting member of Congress so close to an election appear to run afoul of internal Justice Department guidelines, which state that prosecutors and agents should avoid taking overt investigative steps that could affect the outcome of an election or give one candidate an advantage or disadvantage.
Omar's lawyers also raised these same concerns in their letter to the department, saying: "Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions. But the political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day. For the reasons given above, this search was neither justified nor lawful."
Omar has long been a frequent political target by President Trump and his allies. Mr. Trump has also made derogatory comments about her Somali heritage and her religion, and he has repeatedly accused her of immigration fraud.
"There is no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status," her attorneys wrote in the letter to DOJ, adding the search of her home "arose from a years-old, tired conspiracy theory concerning conduct stretching back decades."
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin made unusually public remarks about the nonpublic criminal investigation in a podcast on Friday, calling it a "strong case."
In an interview with Andrew Kolvet, who hosts "The Charlie Kirk Show," Mullin volunteered that multiple warrants had been served on Monday, adding that a judge had authorized the enforcement action and investigators expected to present their case to a grand jury.
It is unusual for federal officials to speak openly about ongoing criminal investigations beyond confirming a court-authorized search was conducted, in part due to due process protections and grand jury secrecy rules.

sources.news_title: Ilhan Omar’s lawyers demand the return of property seized in house raid
sources.text:
Ilhan Omar’s lawyers demand the return of property seized in house raid
Omar’s legal team says the search violated safeguards designed to protect constitutional rights of members of Congress.
Lawyers for Democratic United States Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota have demanded the return of property seized in a federal raid of her Washington, DC home, accusing the US Department of Justice of conducting a politically motivated investigation and failing to follow judicial instructions during the search.
“The political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day,” Omar’s lawyers wrote in a letter sent to federal prosecutors on Friday and obtained by The Associated Press news agency. “This search was neither justified nor lawful.”
In the letter, Omar’s lawyers, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, challenged an investigation into her immigration history, saying there was “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status”.
The letter accuses federal agents of threatening the separation of powers and failing to comply with a magistrate judge’s instructions for the search of Omar’s northeast Washington home on Monday.
Federal agents searched Omar’s home on Monday as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud. Authorities seized her phone and passport, and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, according to The Washington Post. Her lawyers also asked authorities to preserve audio and video recordings from the search.
Omar’s lawyers claim that investigators did not provide a copy of the warrant to them in advance, nor did they contact the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel, which disregarded the magistrate judge’s orders. The notice would have allowed Omar to seek legal counsel and potentially leverage legislation that could have challenged the warrant.
Her lawyers said the procedures outlined by the judge are intended to protect Omar’s constitutional rights as a sitting member of Congress, and safeguard against the seizure of materials related to her legislative work.
Her lawyers also argued that the investigation was politically motivated due to its proximity to the November midterm elections.
“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions,” they wrote.
The Justice Department rejected the accusations, describing the letter as “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies”.
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said.
Omar became a naturalised US citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia with her family as a child, according to her House biography. She has repeatedly rejected allegations by conservative critics about her immigration status, which was also probed in 2019 during Trump’s first administration.
Omar’s lawyers have requested records relating to the 2019 inquiry into her immigration history. The former investigation found insufficient evidence of wrongdoing to warrant a full investigation, according to The Washington Post.
The scope of the current investigation remains unclear.
The search took place days after Trump attacked Omar at a rally in Tennessee, describing her home country as a place of “crime and squalor” and suggesting that Vice President JD Vance and others were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump denied any involvement, telling reporters the matter was “really up to the DOJ”.

sources.news_title: Rep. Ilhan Omar's Attorneys Demand Return Of Property Seized In Federal Search Of Her Home
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Attorneys for Rep. Ilhan Omar asked the Justice Department on Friday to immediately return property that federal agents seized from her home this week, arguing that the search stemming from an immigration fraud investigation was “neither justified nor lawful.”
In a letter obtained by The Associated Press, lawyers for the Democrat from Minnesota described the investigation as a baseless effort to go after a longtime political target of Republican President Donald Trump, noting that the search was conducted just weeks before the midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.
Omar’s attorneys wrote that there is “no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status.”
“This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the President’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers,” Omar’s legal team wrote in the letter first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
A Justice Department spokesperson said the letter from Omar’s defense team was “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies.”
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” department spokesperson Emily Covington wrote in a text message Friday evening.
Monday’s search of Omar’s Washington, D.C., home this week drew swift condemnation from Democrats, as the Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Federal authorities seized Omar’s phone in the search and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the probe told the AP this week.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family’s immigration paperwork. Separately, Washington’s U.S Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said “there are several investigations going on” related to Omar and her office is probing issues concerning the lawmaker’s financial disclosures.
In the letter, Omar’s attorneys accused the Justice Department of violating longstanding agency policy designed to avoid potentially influencing an election. They also raised concerns about whether the department appropriately followed all of the specific instructions by the magistrate judge who approved the search.
In addition to the return of her property, Omar’s attorneys are demanding that the Justice Department preserve any audio and video that was taken during the search, according to the letter.
Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress.
According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia’s civil war when she was 8: “The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family.” She became a lawfully naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.
Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies” and called the insinuation “absurd and offensive.”
The search of her home came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of “crime and squalor” and suggested that Vice President JD Vance “and our people” were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had “nothing to do” with it and it’s “really up to the DOJ.”

sources.news_title: Rep. Ilhan Omar’s lawyers say authorities ignored judge’s restrictions on home search
Rep. Ilhan Omar challenges legality of Trump administration search of her home
sources.text:
Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar is fighting back against the Trump administration’s search of her home earlier this week – disputing its legality and demanding the return of her property seized by federal agents.
Omar’s attorneys sent a letter Friday, obtained by CNN, to prosecutors at the Justice Department, saying, “This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the President’s chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar’s constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers.”
The administration pushed for an unusually aggressive search of Omar’s Washington, DC-area house in an immigration fraud probe that targets the congresswoman, possible false statements made on government documents, and a potential conspiracy, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation. Federal officers executed a search warrant early Monday after a federal magistrate judge signed off on the warrant, while limiting how the Justice Department could access her documents. Omar has been the persistent target of ire from President Donald Trump’s administration.
Omar sought to dismantle the basis of the probe, saying she became a lawfully naturalized citizen in 2000 after fleeing Somalia in 1995.
“There is no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status,” Omar’s attorneys, Amy Jeffress and Joshua Matz, wrote in the letter to federal prosecutors. They also demanded that all video and audio recordings made by federal agents during the search be preserved.
A Justice Department spokesperson told CNN in a statement that the letter from Omar’s attorneys was “riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies.”
“Our attorneys and law enforcement partners complied with all court orders and legal obligations, as they always do,” the spokesperson said in the statement to CNN. “Leaking a letter to the press right after sending it is not good faith. It is a publicity play.”
Omar’s attorneys pointed out a number of issues with how the search of Omar’s home was conducted. They said the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel was not notified about the search until after it was publicly reported. The judge in Washington had mandated special procedures about giving notice to the House and to Omar and her attorneys about her Constitutional protections as a member of Congress, the letter said. Omar’s defense attorneys indicated the investigators may have infringed on the congresswoman’s rights by not following the judge’s parameters.
There also was no one from the US attorney’s office or the Justice Department at the search to read Omar her privileges under the Speech or Debate Clause, according to the letter, and instead Omar was presented with a waiver that she did not sign. Omar’s attorneys also alleged they did not have the opportunity to identify or segregate materials that were protected under the clause.
The search “arose from a years-old, tired conspiracy theory,” Omar’s attorneys wrote, also pointing out the search was conducted less than three weeks before Election Day.
“Historically, the Department has refrained from this type of investigative activity so close to an election, so as to avoid even the appearance of politically motivated law enforcement actions. But the political motivations behind this pre-election investigation and search are clear as day. For the reasons given above, this search was neither justified nor lawful,” they wrote in the letter, first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
Jeffress and Matz noted that Omar was repeatedly referred to by her first name in the search warrant paperwork and called on the agents to respect the congresswoman with her proper title going forward.
Katelyn Polantz contributed to this report.
This story has been updated.
